CHEMISTRY MASTER CORPUS — DEEP EDITION
=======================================

SCOPE
-----
This corpus is designed as a broad chemistry knowledge/training corpus covering:

• Grades 7–10 foundation and secondary chemistry
• Grades 11–12 NCERT/CBSE-style senior-secondary chemistry
• Indian higher-education progression through B.Sc. Chemistry
• M.Sc. Chemistry and advanced research-oriented chemistry
• Physical, inorganic, organic and analytical chemistry
• Quantum chemistry, thermodynamics, kinetics and equilibrium
• Coordination, ligand-field, organometallic and bioinorganic chemistry
• Organic mechanisms, stereochemistry, heterocycles, pericyclic and asymmetric chemistry
• Chromatography, electroanalysis, thermal analysis, IR, Raman, UV-Vis, NMR, MS, EPR and Mössbauer
• Periodicity and a 118-element reference directory
• Nuclear, materials, green, environmental, industrial and pharmaceutical chemistry

DESIGN OF EACH TOPIC ENTRY
--------------------------
Each topic contains:
1. Definition
2. Deep theory / explanation
3. Core concepts
4. Key equations / relationships
5. Applications
6. Comparisons
7. Laboratory / analytical examples
8. EXACTLY 15 varied examples
9. 5 common misconceptions
10. Prerequisites
11. Difficulty
12. Safety/context notes
13. Five question-answer prompts at Easy, Medium, Mechanistic, Application and Reasoning levels

ELEMENT DIRECTORY
-----------------
The periodic-table section provides one structured entry for every element from
H (1) through Og (118), with atomic number, representative mass/isotope notation,
electron configuration, classification, representative oxidation states,
representative compounds, applications/relevance, comparison prompts and
educational examples.

SOURCE INTEGRATION
------------------
The user's supplied chemistry roadmap is the primary curriculum specification.
Additional attached chemistry material was incorporated where relevant, including
the 118-element master-directory framework, quantum atomic structure, effective
nuclear charge, extraction/metallurgy, nuclear chemistry, Grade 11 mole concept,
Grade 12 electrochemistry and related teaching-corpus structures. The attached
material explicitly describes a 118-element directory and the quantum/electronic
structure and periodicity framework. fileciteturn7file4L202-L219
The attached Grade 11 corpus also includes mole/stoichiometry teaching material
and quantum-structure records. fileciteturn6file3L120-L134
The Grade 12 corpus contains an electrochemistry anchor covering galvanic and
electrolytic cells, Nernst equation, conductance and Faraday laws. fileciteturn6file14L636-L640

QUALITY / SAFETY NOTE
---------------------
This is an educational corpus rather than a laboratory manual. Equations and
reaction descriptions are intended for learning. Radioactive, toxic, corrosive,
flammable, high-pressure and otherwise hazardous chemistry must be handled only
under appropriate institutional controls and qualified supervision.

TOTAL STRUCTURED ENTRIES: 207
TOTAL ELEMENT ENTRIES: 118

ENTRY 0001
LEVEL      : Grade 7
DISCIPLINE : General Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Acids, Bases and Salts
TOPIC      : Indicators
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
An indicator is a substance whose observable property, commonly colour, changes with acidity or basicity.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Indicator molecules have protonation states with different structures and colours. Natural indicators such as turmeric and litmus provide qualitative classification; laboratory indicators such as phenolphthalein and methyl orange provide sharper transition ranges.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Acidic solution
2. Basic solution
3. Indicator transition
4. Hydrogen-ion activity
5. Neutralization

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. pH = -log10(aH+)
2. n = m/M

5. APPLICATIONS
1. testing household substances
2. acid-base titration introduction
3. qualitative laboratory analysis

6. COMPARISONS
1. litmus vs turmeric
2. phenolphthalein vs methyl orange

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES
1. test acid/base samples with litmus
2. observe turmeric colour change
3. compare indicator endpoints

8. FIFTEEN DETAILED EXAMPLES
1. Worked/example 1 — Core identification: Acidic solution is directly observed when studying Indicators.
2. Worked/example 2 — Mechanism: Basic solution explains why a chemical system behaves as it does in Indicators.
3. Worked/example 3 — Quantitative use: pH = -log10(aH+) can be used when solving a Indicators problem.
4. Worked/example 4 — Laboratory context: test acid/base samples with litmus illustrates Indicators experimentally.
5. Worked/example 5 — Real-world application: testing household substances uses principles of Indicators.
6. Worked/example 6 — Comparison: litmus vs turmeric differs from the alternative because of its underlying chemistry.
7. Worked/example 7 — Mechanistic extension: Indicator transition becomes important when conditions change.
8. Worked/example 8 — Calculation/interpretation: n = m/M provides a useful quantitative relationship.
9. Worked/example 9 — Laboratory context: observe turmeric colour change can be used to investigate Indicators.
10. Worked/example 10 — Application: acid-base titration introduction demonstrates how Indicators extends beyond textbook chemistry.
11. Worked/example 11 — Comparison: phenolphthalein vs methyl orange highlights a structural or energetic distinction in Indicators.
12. Worked/example 12 — Advanced connection: Hydrogen-ion activity connects Indicators with another branch of chemistry.
13. Worked/example 13 — Analytical interpretation: compare indicator endpoints produces data that can be interpreted using Indicators.
14. Worked/example 14 — Applied chemistry: qualitative laboratory analysis depends on controlling a variable associated with Indicators.
15. Worked/example 15 — Synthesis/reasoning: Neutralization can be used to predict, explain or design a chemical outcome involving Indicators.

9. COMMON MISCONCEPTIONS
1. Confusing the definition of Indicators with a related but different concept.
2. Assuming that every example of Indicators behaves ideally.
3. Using a formula for Indicators outside the assumptions under which it was derived.
4. Treating a macroscopic observation as proof of only one microscopic mechanism.
5. Ignoring units, stoichiometry, charge balance or limiting conditions.

ENTRY 0002
LEVEL      : Grade 7
DISCIPLINE : General Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Acids, Bases and Salts
TOPIC      : Neutralization
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Neutralization is an acid-base reaction in which acidic and basic species react to form less acidic/basic products, often including water and a salt.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
In aqueous strong acid/strong base reactions, H3O+ and OH− combine to form water. The net ionic equation is H3O+ + OH− → 2H2O.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Acid
2. Base
3. Salt
4. Neutralization
5. Heat of neutralization

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. H+ + OH− → H2O
2. q = mcΔT

5. APPLICATIONS
1. antacids
2. soil treatment
3. industrial pH control

6. COMPARISONS
1. strong acid/strong base
2. weak acid/strong base

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES
1. HCl with NaOH
2. vinegar with sodium bicarbonate
3. measure temperature during neutralization

8. FIFTEEN DETAILED EXAMPLES
1. Worked/example 1 — Core identification: Acid is directly observed when studying Neutralization.

ENTRY 0003
LEVEL      : Grade 7
DISCIPLINE : General Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Physical and Chemical Changes
TOPIC      : Physical change
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
A physical change alters physical form or state without changing the chemical identity of the substance.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Melting, freezing, boiling, grinding and dissolving can occur without formation of a new chemical species, although dissolution can involve molecular interactions and is not always simply reversible.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. State change
2. Phase transition
3. Reversibility
4. Physical property
5. Composition

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. q = mL
2. density = mass/volume

5. APPLICATIONS
1. ice storage
2. distillation
3. crystallization

6. COMPARISONS
1. melting vs burning
2. boiling vs decomposition

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES
1. melt ice
2. evaporate water
3. crystallize salt

8. FIFTEEN DETAILED EXAMPLES

ENTRY 0004
LEVEL      : Grade 7
DISCIPLINE : General Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Physical and Chemical Changes
TOPIC      : Chemical change
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
A chemical change produces one or more substances with chemical compositions different from the starting materials.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Chemical reactions rearrange atoms through bond breaking, bond formation and electron transfer or sharing. Evidence can include gas evolution, precipitate formation, colour change or heat release, but none alone proves a specific mechanism.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Reactant
2. Product
3. Chemical equation
4. Bond rearrangement
5. Reaction evidence

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. mass balance
2. stoichiometric ratio

5. APPLICATIONS
1. rusting
2. food digestion
3. combustion

6. COMPARISONS
1. chemical vs physical change
2. oxidation vs simple colour change

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES

2. vinegar and carbonate
3. burn a supervised fuel sample

ENTRY 0005
LEVEL      : Grade 8
DISCIPLINE : General Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Polymers
TOPIC      : Synthetic fibers and polymers
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
A polymer is a macromolecule composed of repeating structural units derived from monomers or monomer-like precursors.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Addition polymerization commonly joins unsaturated monomers, while condensation polymerization forms polymers with loss of small molecules in many systems. Polymer properties depend on chain length, branching, crystallinity and cross-linking.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Monomer
2. Polymer
3. Degree of polymerization
4. Addition polymerization
5. Condensation polymerization

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. DP ≈ polymer molecular mass/repeat-unit mass
2. yield = product/expected product ×100

5. APPLICATIONS
1. nylon
2. polyester
3. polyethylene products

6. COMPARISONS
1. thermoplastic vs thermoset
2. addition vs condensation

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES
1. polymer solubility comparison
2. fiber strength comparison
3. observe thermoplastic softening under controlled conditions

LEVEL      : Grade 8
DISCIPLINE : General Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Metals and Non-metals
TOPIC      : Metallic properties
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Metallic elements commonly exhibit electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, malleability and ductility because of their bonding and electronic structure.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Metallic bonding involves delocalized valence electrons interacting with positive ion cores. Chemical reactivity depends on ionization energy, lattice/solvation effects and redox potentials.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Metallic bond
2. Ductility
3. Malleability
4. Electrical conductivity
5. Redox tendency

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS

2. Ecell = Ecathode − Eanode

5. APPLICATIONS

2. construction
3. electroplating

6. COMPARISONS

ENTRY 0007
LEVEL      : Grade 8
DISCIPLINE : General Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Metals and Non-metals
TOPIC      : Displacement reactions
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive species replaces a less reactive species in a compound.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Metal displacement is governed by relative redox tendencies. A metal with a more negative reduction potential can often reduce ions of a less active metal under appropriate conditions.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Reactivity series
2. Oxidation
3. Reduction
4. Single displacement
5. Electrochemical potential

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. Ecell = Ecathode − Eanode
2. ΔG = −nFE

5. APPLICATIONS
1. metal recovery
2. corrosion studies
3. qualitative analysis

6. COMPARISONS
1. single vs double displacement
2. thermodynamic feasibility vs reaction rate

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES

ENTRY 0015
LEVEL      : Grade 10
DISCIPLINE : General/Organic/Inorganic Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Chemical Reactions and Equations
TOPIC      : Chemical equation balancing
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
A balanced chemical equation represents a reaction with equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Coefficients are adjusted to satisfy conservation of atoms; subscripts are not changed because they define the substances.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Reactant coefficients
2. Product coefficients
3. Conservation of mass
4. State symbols
5. Reaction conditions

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. aA+bB→cC
2. moles product = stoichiometric coefficient ratio

5. APPLICATIONS
1. industrial material balances
2. laboratory reaction planning
3. combustion calculations

6. COMPARISONS
1. balancing vs changing formulae
2. coefficient vs subscript

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES

2. balance combustion
3. balance redox reaction

CHAPTER    : Some Basic Concepts
TOPIC      : Stoichiometry and limiting reagent
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Stoichiometry quantifies reactant-product relationships, while the limiting reagent is the reactant consumed first under the specified stoichiometric conditions.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
A balanced equation supplies mole ratios. Comparing available moles divided by stoichiometric coefficients identifies the limiting reagent and therefore the theoretical product amount.

3. CORE CONCEPTS

2. Limiting reagent
3. Excess reagent
4. Theoretical yield
5. Percent yield

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS

2. reagent planning
3. laboratory synthesis

CHAPTER    : Thermodynamics
TOPIC      : Entropy and Gibbs energy
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Entropy quantifies the dispersal of energy and matter in a thermodynamic description; Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy for constant-temperature, constant-pressure spontaneity criteria.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
For a process at constant T and P, negative ΔG indicates thermodynamic spontaneity in the chosen direction, while equilibrium corresponds to ΔG = 0.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Entropy
2. Gibbs energy
3. Spontaneity
4. Equilibrium
5. Reversibility

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
2. ΔG° = −RT ln K

5. APPLICATIONS
1. reaction feasibility
2. phase transitions
3. electrochemistry

6. COMPARISONS
1. spontaneous vs fast
2. ΔG vs activation energy

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES

TOPIC      : Chemical equilibrium
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state in which forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and macroscopic composition remains constant.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
The equilibrium constant depends on temperature and is expressed using activities or approximations such as concentrations/partial pressures under defined conditions. Le Chatelier's principle predicts qualitative responses to perturbations.

1. DEFINITION
Electrochemistry studies chemical reactions involving electron transfer and their relationship to electrical potential and current.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Galvanic cells convert spontaneous chemical free energy into electrical work; electrolytic cells use electrical energy to drive nonspontaneous processes. Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode in both cases.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Anode
2. Cathode
3. Salt bridge
4. EMF
5. Electrolysis

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. Ecell = Ecathode − Eanode
2. ΔG = −nFE

5. APPLICATIONS
1. batteries
2. electroplating
3. fuel cells

6. COMPARISONS
1. galvanic vs electrolytic
2. anode/cathode sign conventions

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES
1. Daniell cell
2. electrolysis
3. cell-potential calculation

8. FIFTEEN DETAILED EXAMPLES
1. Worked/example 1 — Core identification: Anode is directly observed when studying Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
2. Worked/example 2 — Mechanism: Cathode explains why a chemical system behaves as it does in Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
3. Worked/example 3 — Quantitative use: Ecell = Ecathode − Eanode can be used when solving a Galvanic and electrolytic cells problem.
4. Worked/example 4 — Laboratory context: Daniell cell illustrates Galvanic and electrolytic cells experimentally.
5. Worked/example 5 — Real-world application: batteries uses principles of Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
6. Worked/example 6 — Comparison: galvanic vs electrolytic differs from the alternative because of its underlying chemistry.
7. Worked/example 7 — Mechanistic extension: Salt bridge becomes important when conditions change.
8. Worked/example 8 — Calculation/interpretation: ΔG = −nFE provides a useful quantitative relationship.
9. Worked/example 9 — Laboratory context: electrolysis can be used to investigate Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
10. Worked/example 10 — Application: electroplating demonstrates how Galvanic and electrolytic cells extends beyond textbook chemistry.
11. Worked/example 11 — Comparison: anode/cathode sign conventions highlights a structural or energetic distinction in Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
12. Worked/example 12 — Advanced connection: EMF connects Galvanic and electrolytic cells with another branch of chemistry.
13. Worked/example 13 — Analytical interpretation: cell-potential calculation produces data that can be interpreted using Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
14. Worked/example 14 — Applied chemistry: fuel cells depends on controlling a variable associated with Galvanic and electrolytic cells.
15. Worked/example 15 — Synthesis/reasoning: Electrolysis can be used to predict, explain or design a chemical outcome involving Galvanic and electrolytic cells.

9. COMMON MISCONCEPTIONS
1. Confusing the definition of Galvanic and electrolytic cells with a related but different concept.
2. Assuming that every example of Galvanic and electrolytic cells behaves ideally.
3. Using a formula for Galvanic and electrolytic cells outside the assumptions under which it was derived.
4. Treating a macroscopic observation as proof of only one microscopic mechanism.
5. Ignoring units, stoichiometry, charge balance or limiting conditions.

ENTRY 0038
LEVEL      : Grade 12
DISCIPLINE : Physical Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Electrochemistry
TOPIC      : Nernst equation
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
The Nernst equation relates electrode or cell potential to composition and temperature under specified conditions.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
It follows from the thermodynamic relationship between Gibbs energy and reaction quotient and explains concentration dependence of electrochemical potential.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Reaction quotient
2. Standard potential
3. Nonstandard potential
4. Cell potential
5. Electrochemical equilibrium

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. E = E° − RT/(nF) ln Q
2. at 298 K: E = E° − 0.0591/n log Q

5. APPLICATIONS
1. battery state-of-charge
2. ion-selective electrodes
3. corrosion analysis

6. COMPARISONS
1. standard vs nonstandard potential
2. EMF vs terminal voltage

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES
1. Zn/Cu Nernst calculation
2. concentration cell
3. ion activity effect

TOPIC      : Reaction rate and order
DIFFICULTY : Progressive

1. DEFINITION
Chemical kinetics studies how fast reactions occur and how rate depends on concentrations, temperature, catalysts and mechanisms.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Rate laws are empirical or mechanistically derived relationships. Reaction order is determined from concentration dependence; molecularity refers to an elementary step.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Rate
2. Order
3. Molecularity
4. Rate constant
5. Half-life

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. rate = k[A]^m[B]^n
2. first-order t1/2 = 0.693/k

5. APPLICATIONS
1. drug degradation
2. industrial reactors
3. environmental chemistry

6. COMPARISONS
1. order vs molecularity
2. rate vs equilibrium

TOPIC      : SN1 and SN2 substitution
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Nucleophilic substitution replaces a leaving group with a nucleophile through one-step or multistep mechanisms.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
SN2 is concerted and gives inversion at a stereogenic center; SN1 proceeds through a carbocation intermediate and can give mixtures due to planar intermediates.

3. CORE CONCEPTS

2. SN2
3. Leaving group
4. Nucleophile
5. Carbocation

ENTRY 0044
LEVEL      : Grade 12
DISCIPLINE : Organic Chemistry
CHAPTER    : Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
TOPIC      : Oxygen-containing functional groups
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Alcohols, phenols and ethers contain carbon-oxygen single bonds but differ substantially in acidity, hydrogen bonding and reaction pathways.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Phenols are more acidic than typical aliphatic alcohols because phenoxide is resonance-stabilized. Ethers are comparatively less reactive but can undergo cleavage under strong conditions.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Alcohol
2. Phenol
3. Ether
4. Hydrogen bonding
5. Phenoxide

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. pKa comparison
2. Williamson ether synthesis

5. APPLICATIONS
1. solvents
2. antiseptics
3. fragrance chemistry

6. COMPARISONS
1. phenol vs alcohol acidity
2. ether vs alcohol boiling point

7. LABORATORY / ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES
1. Lucas-type classification
2. esterification
3. ether preparation

TOPIC      : Chemical potential and fugacity
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Chemical potential is the partial molar Gibbs energy and determines the direction of matter transfer and phase/reaction equilibrium.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
For ideal gases, chemical potential depends logarithmically on pressure. Fugacity generalizes pressure for real gases and allows thermodynamic equations to retain ideal-gas-like form.

2. Partial molar quantity
3. Fugacity
4. Activity
5. Gibbs-Duhem equation

5. APPLICATIONS

2. activity vs concentration

TOPIC      : Vibrational spectroscopy
DIFFICULTY : Progressive

Vibrational spectroscopy probes quantized molecular vibrations through interaction with electromagnetic radiation.

IR activity requires a changing dipole moment; Raman activity requires a changing polarizability. Centrosymmetric molecules can obey mutual exclusion between IR and Raman activity for normal modes.

TOPIC      : Hartree-Fock SCF
DIFFICULTY : Progressive

1. DEFINITION
Hartree-Fock theory approximates a many-electron wavefunction using antisymmetrized products of one-electron orbitals optimized self-consistently.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Each electron moves in an average field generated by the nuclei and other electrons. The Fock operator is solved iteratively until the orbitals and density converge.

TOPIC      : Radioactive decay
DIFFICULTY : Progressive
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION
Radioactive decay is the spontaneous transformation of an unstable atomic nucleus into another nuclear state or nuclide with emission of radiation.

2. DEEP THEORY / EXPLANATION
Alpha, beta and gamma processes differ in emitted radiation and changes in nuclear composition. Decay is stochastic for individual nuclei but predictable statistically using half-life.

3. CORE CONCEPTS
1. Nuclide
2. Half-life
3. Alpha decay
4. Beta decay
5. Gamma emission

4. KEY EQUATIONS / RELATIONSHIPS
1. N(t)=N0 e^(−λt)
2. t1/2 = ln2/λ
